strengths: Introduces the first multiview object-level change detection benchmark with video pairs and dense instance annotations; the task and dataset address a real gap relative to RC-3D, 3DGS-CD, and PASLCD.

The dataset contains 350 sequence pairs across 20 scene categories with Added/Removed/Moved labels, object attributes, and a SAM2-based annotation tool; public release would be valuable for the community.
The evaluation protocol distinguishes per-view and per-scene evaluation and type-aware AP, explicitly acknowledging ambiguity between detecting changes and classifying change types.

The training-free SceneDiff method sensibly combines foundation models (pi3, SAM, DINOv3) with geometry, appearance, and region cues, plus co-visibility pairing and instance association; it outperforms baselines on the proposed benchmark, RC-3D, and ChangeSim.

The paper includes ablations over geometry models and feature cues, qualitative comparisons, failure-case analysis, and a robotic tidying demonstration, which support the empirical claims and expose limitations.
The manuscript is generally well organized and provides substantial supplementary details on implementation, annotation, baselines, and failure modes.
Reproducibility is partly addressed through planned release of data, annotation tool, and code, along with implementation details for baselines.
weaknesses: Benchmark scale and diversity are modest: 350 video pairs and roughly 1009 changed objects, not 'thousands' as the abstract states; only 50 scenes are used, and 150 pairs come from HD-Epic, potentially biasing SD-K toward egocentric cooking scenes.

It is unclear how the dataset avoids dynamic content such as hands, people, or pets in HD-Epic cooking sequences, despite claiming that no dynamic objects are captured; this could affect annotation validity and task framing.

The point-based evaluation converts predictions to centroids and checks containment in ground-truth boxes, ignoring localization and segmentation quality; allowing two duplicate detections per ground truth without penalty may inflate AP, and the AP computation is not formally defined in the main paper.

The method is largely an engineering composition of off-the-shelf models with many hand-tuned thresholds and weights; technical novelty is limited, and sensitivity/robustness to these hyperparameters is only partially analyzed.

Baseline fairness is questionable: 3DGS-CD is adapted by dropping its occupancy grid and changing camera poses/sampling, the VLM baseline may be bottlenecked by Grounding SAM localization, and CYWS-3D is given pi3 depth and custom pairing; the large margins may partly reflect baseline limitations rather than method superiority.

The ablation results show inconsistency: Ef+Er achieves higher APtype than the full model on SD-V, and the contribution of E_region is small, so the claimed role of region matching needs clarification.
Runtime is high at 159.4s per sequence pair, making the method impractical for online robotics; the robot demonstration is qualitative and lacks success-rate, cycle-time, or closed-loop evaluation.

Annotation quality is not quantified: no inter-annotator agreement, annotation error analysis, or handling of SAM2 propagation failures is reported; moved-object correspondence and occlusion handling across videos remain unclear.

The method inherits failure modes of pi3 and SAM under low overlap, strong lighting changes, textureless surfaces, and cluttered repetitive scenes; these are acknowledged but not mitigated, and no uncertainty estimate is provided.

Reproducibility is incomplete at review time: code, data, and exact evaluation scripts are only promised upon acceptance, while AP details and several baseline adaptations are relegated to the supplement and remain underspecified.

strengths: Introduces SceneDiff Benchmark, a substantial new dataset: 350 before/after video pairs (200 manually collected SD-V, 150 from HD-Epic SD-K), 1009 changed objects, instance masks, and Added/Removed/Moved labels; it fills a real gap compared with similar-viewpoint or semantic-only change-detection benchmarks.

Provides a careful SAM2-based annotation tool and a per-view/per-scene evaluation protocol with AP and AP_type, including object association across views; the dataset, tool, and code are promised for release.

Proposes a training-free pipeline that leverages pre-trained geometry (π³), segmentation (SAM), and appearance (DINOv3) models; the design is plausible and the ablations support the importance of appearance features and geometry models.
Reports large improvements over baselines on the proposed benchmark and strong results on RC-3D and ChangeSim; the robotic tidying demonstration illustrates a meaningful downstream use case.

Acknowledges important limitations, including ambiguous identical-object swaps, geometry-reconstruction failures under low overlap or strong lighting changes, and semantic state changes as future work.
weaknesses: The method's region-association equation for S_geo as printed is inconsistent: it sums over points in the object point cloud and computes the minimum distance to points in the same object point cloud, making the indicator nearly always true. The text describes a region-to-object distance, so the formula should involve the region's point cloud instead. This undermines reproducibility and the association step as written.

Key implementation details are missing or underspecified: voxel size for 3D score aggregation, how prediction confidence is computed for AP, exactly how AP is calculated, and how hyperparameters (τ_occ, λ^g/λ^f/λ^r, σ_geo, σ_merge, τ_sim) were chosen and how sensitive results are to them. Ablations are mostly restricted to SD-V and do not cover the full scoring weights or association thresholds.

Benchmark split validity is unclear: 350 sequence pairs come from only 50 scenes, but the paper does not state that train/val/test splits are scene-disjoint. If the same scene appears in validation and test, results can be inflated. There is also no true training split, only 50 validation pairs per subset described as intended for training or hyperparameter tuning.

The evaluation metric is lenient and not fully justified: ground-truth masks are reduced to bounding boxes, any detection point inside a box counts as TP, and up to two detection points per ground truth are allowed without penalty. This can overstate detection performance and does not measure segmentation quality, despite the dataset providing masks.

Baselines are limited or weak: the VLM + Grounding SAM baseline is not a strong change-detection method; 3DGS-CD is heavily adapted and reported at near-zero performance; CYWS-3D is a two-view method that cannot perform multi-view association, so only per-view AP is reported. The proposed benchmark also lacks comparisons to several recent relevant methods.

Absolute performance remains low, especially on SD-K (per-scene AP 20.9, AP_type 12.2), which undercuts claims of robust multiview change detection and practical readiness. The paper acknowledges this only partially.

Dataset annotation quality is insufficiently validated: SAM2-assisted masks may contain errors, but no inter-annotator agreement, annotation accuracy, or quality-control statistics are reported. The abstract's mention of 'thousands of changed objects' is not supported by the reported 1009 annotated objects.

Reproducibility and clarity are weakened by missing or unclear details: code/data are not yet available, the method depends on many pre-trained models and thresholds, and several equations/terms are unclear (e.g., the definition of F_pre^* and the asymmetric threshold τ_occ despite the stated non-negative rule).

strengths: The paper makes a significant benchmark contribution: SceneDiff is the first multiview change detection benchmark with object instance annotations over video pairs, with 350 pairs, 1009 changed objects, two subsets, dense masks/change types, an annotation tool, and per-view/per-scene evaluation protocol. This addresses a clear gap in real-world multiview change detection.

The proposed training-free method is well motivated and technically coherent: it leverages pretrained geometry (π³), segmentation (SAM), and semantic features (DINOv3), combines asymmetric depth-reprojection, appearance, and region-matching cues, then aggregates/associates regions into object-level changes. The pipeline is described clearly and is reproducible in principle.

Experiments show substantial gains over adapted baselines on both SceneDiff Benchmark and RC-3D (e.g., 49.6 vs 26.9 per-view AP on SD-V; 68.7 AP50 on RC-3D), plus ChangeSim results and a robot demonstration, supporting practical impact. Ablations reasonably test geometry models, feature backbones, and cue contributions.

The paper is generally clear, includes important supplementary details, appropriately attributes prior work, and promises code/data release. Limitations and failure cases are discussed, which helps contextualize the claims.
weaknesses: The point-based evaluation converts masks/boxes to centroids and allows up to two detections per ground truth without penalty; while justified by annotation ambiguity, this is non-standard and may be permissive, and it does not directly measure segmentation quality despite the dense instance masks.

Baseline comparisons involve considerable adaptation (e.g., custom poses/thresholds for 3DGS-CD, π³ depth for CYWS-3D, GroundingSAM for VLM), so the reported margins may partly reflect baseline setup rather than inherent limitations. Stronger or more standardized baselines would strengthen the claims.

The method is training-free but depends on several large pretrained models and manually tuned hyperparameters/thresholds (λ, τ_Δ, σ_merge, etc.), with high inference cost (159.4s per sequence; SAM 4s per image). It is also brittle to reconstruction failure, lighting changes, and repetitive cluttered objects, as the paper notes.

Per-scene type-aware performance remains low (25.5 AP_type on SD-V, 12.2 on SD-K), and Moved object association/classification appears particularly difficult. The benchmark is relatively modest in scene diversity (50 scenes/20 categories), which may limit generalization claims.

The method's novelty is mainly in combining existing foundation models and region-level scoring; the paper could more deeply analyze failure modes and provide more standardized metrics (e.g., mask AP) to support the benchmark as a lasting evaluation resource.

strengths: Introduces a substantial new benchmark for multiview object change detection with 350 real-world video sequence pairs, dense instance-level annotations, consistent cross-view object IDs, and per-view/per-scene evaluation metrics, filling an important gap between two-view similar-viewpoint datasets and dense-view 3DGS-based benchmarks.

Provides a SAM2-based annotation tool, data collection guidelines, evaluation protocol, and codebase/dataset release plan, making the benchmark a useful community resource rather than only a method paper.

The proposed training-free SceneDiff method is simple and well motivated: it performs co-visibility-based frame pairing, asymmetric depth-reprojection scoring, DINO-feature appearance comparison, region-level matching, and cross-view object association using pretrained foundation models.

Experimental evidence is strong on the proposed benchmark and RC-3D, with large reported improvements over adapted baselines; additional results on PASLCD and ChangeSim show reasonable generalization, and ablations/sensitivity analyses support key design choices.

The paper is clearly written, includes extensive supplementary material, provides implementation details for baselines, and acknowledges meaningful limitations such as ambiguous swaps, geometry failures, and semantic state changes.
weaknesses: The claim of being the "first multiview change detection dataset" is somewhat overclaimed: prior datasets such as 3DGS-CD and PASLCD already provide different-viewpoint or dense multiview captures. The actual novelty is better described as the first instance-level multiview benchmark with consistent cross-view IDs.

The benchmark scale is moderate: 200 manually collected sequence pairs from 7 people plus 150 from HD-Epic, spanning 50 scenes. No inter-annotator agreement or annotation-quality statistics are reported, which limits confidence in annotation reliability and scene diversity.

Baseline comparisons involve many adaptations that may affect fairness: using the authors' π³ poses for 3DGS-CD/MV3DCD, disabling 3DGS-CD's occupancy-grid output, fine-tuning CYWS-2D on the authors' validation set, and using SAM3 for VLM localization. These choices are discussed, but a more controlled oracle/adaptation study would strengthen the comparison.

The ablation in Table 5 is somewhat at odds with the paper's stated priorities: the variant without geometry (Ef+Er) improves obj/sc AP by +2.6 and obj/im AP by +0.9 over the full method, while geometry-only scoring hurts scene-level AP. Since obj/sc AP is described as the most important metric, this tension needs clearer justification or a stronger selection rationale.

The method relies on joint static geometry reconstruction of scenes that contain object changes—precisely the setting that violates the static-scene assumption of models like π³/VGGT. Although the supplement investigates robustness, the main paper does not sufficiently quantify sensitivity to change type, change amount, or low co-visibility, and geometry failure remains a critical failure mode.

Some metric definitions are under-specified in the main paper, e.g., exactly how obj/sc AP aggregates IoU across frames and sequences and how scene-level predictions are ranked. These details matter for reproducibility and should be stated precisely.

The method is computationally expensive at ~159s per sequence pair and depends on several very recent foundation models (π³, DINOv3, SAM3, Qwen2.5-VL) whose public availability/licensing may change over time, creating a reproducibility and deployment risk that is not fully addressed.

strengths: Introduces a potentially useful new benchmark for multiview object-level change detection: 350 video pairs with dense instance annotations, varied camera trajectories, and per-view/per-scene evaluation protocols. The dataset, annotation tool, and evaluation code would be valuable to the community if released.

The proposed SceneDiff method is training-free and leverages strong pretrained foundation models (π³, SAM, DINOv3) without task-specific retraining, making it broadly applicable to image pairs and video sequences.

The paper reports strong empirical results on the proposed benchmark and on the established RC-3D benchmark, and includes ablations, failure-case analysis, hyperparameter sensitivity, and a qualitative robotic demonstration.
The limitations section is candid about ambiguous change configurations and geometry failures, which improves transparency.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is limited: SceneDiff is largely a pipeline that combines off-the-shelf 3D reconstruction, segmentation, and semantic feature models with hand-designed scoring and thresholds. It does not introduce a fundamentally new algorithmic or learning insight; the main novel component is the benchmark and system-level integration.

Baseline comparisons on the proposed benchmark appear potentially unfair or weak. 3DGS-CD's occupancy grid is disabled, 3DGS-based methods are disadvantaged by large view extrapolation, CYWS-2D is finetuned on the validation set, and the VLM baseline uses a crude text-to-SAM3 localization pipeline. The large reported margins may therefore be inflated relative to stronger task-appropriate baselines.

The central scene-level metric, obj/sc AP, is non-standard and not fully specified in the main paper. It requires aggregating per-view detections into object hypotheses, but it is unclear how this association is performed for baselines that do not output object tracks, especially after 3DGS-CD's occupancy grid is disabled. This raises serious concerns about comparability and reproducibility of the headline results.

The ablation study does not convincingly support the paper's claimed importance of the appearance feature cue or the region-matching contribution. For example, E_feat alone gives roughly the same obj/im AP and obj/sc AP as the full model, while E_geom and E_region ablations show mixed effects, so the paper overstates what the ablation demonstrates.

The benchmark lacks a clearly defined training split or protocol for learning-based methods; the paper only describes validation and test splits. It is also unclear how methods requiring training should use the proposed data without violating the benchmark design.

Dataset scale and diversity may be more limited than the paper's framing suggests: 200 manually collected pairs from 7 people and 150 pairs derived from HD-Epic. The core benchmark contribution would benefit from stronger evidence of scene coverage, annotation consistency, and inter-annotator agreement, none of which is quantitatively reported in the main paper.

The robotic application is demonstrated qualitatively but is not quantitatively evaluated (e.g., no success rate, failure statistics, or repeatability analysis), so it provides limited evidence of practical utility.

The paper relies heavily on supplementary material for critical implementation details, metric definitions, and baseline adaptations. Some design choices, such as the asymmetric geometry rule, region exclusion criterion, normalization, and thresholds, are under-justified or ambiguously described in the main text.

strengths: Introduces the first multiview object-level change detection benchmark with 350 real-world video pairs, dense instance annotations, consistent cross-view IDs, diverse indoor/outdoor scenes, an annotation tool, and a defined evaluation protocol.

Defines meaningful metrics spanning pixel/view-level and object/scene-level evaluation, especially obj/sc AP, which addresses the core need to identify the same physical changed object consistently across views.

Proposes a sensible training-free SceneDiff pipeline that co-registers scenes with a feed-forward geometry model, pairs views by co-visibility, scores region-level changes using geometry, appearance, and region-matching cues, and associates regions into object tracks.

Reports strong empirical gains over prior methods on the proposed benchmark (53.0% relative AP improvement) and RC-3D (30.6% relative AP improvement), with competitive results on PASLCD and ChangeSim, supporting the method's effectiveness.

Provides useful ablations and robustness analyses: different geometry/feature models, score components, thresholds, failure cases, and a real robot tidying demonstration, indicating practical relevance.

Reproducibility is supported by a planned release of the dataset, code, annotation tool, and detailed supplementary material including prompts, parameters, running time, and baseline adaptation details.
Limitations are candidly discussed, including ambiguous swaps, pose-estimation failures, lighting changes, and out-of-scope semantic state changes.
weaknesses: Absolute performance remains modest on the hardest settings (e.g., obj/sc AP 10.6 on SD-K), and the method depends heavily on the accuracy of pose and geometry estimation, which can fail under low overlap, extreme lighting, textureless surfaces, or cluttered repetitive scenes.

The training-free pipeline still relies on several manually set thresholds and aggregation choices; although sensitivity analyses are provided, domain transfer may require re-tuning and the approach is less self-contained than a learned end-to-end model.

Some baseline adaptations are non-standard (e.g., 3DGS-based methods are run with regressed poses and modified occupancy handling, and the VLM baseline uses SAM3 with manually matched object names for analysis), so comparison fairness is somewhat difficult to assess despite the authors' justifications.
The benchmark is a strong contribution but moderate in scale (350 video pairs, ~1009 annotated objects) and lacks reported annotation reliability statistics such as inter-annotator agreement.
Semantic state changes and fine-grained deformations are explicitly excluded, which limits the scope of the task formulation even though this exclusion is reasonable for the paper's focus.
